name: Rosa Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fine by me. I'm not much of a talker, but I'll tell you straight. Just don't put my boss's name in anything.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a new housing estate at the edge of town, about sixty houses going up on what used to be a cabbage field. I work for a small framing outfit, so I carry studs, cut noggins, hold the other end of things and nail off sheathing once the lads have stood the walls up. I'm still learning, honestly; I can frame a simple wall now but the roofs and stairs are beyond me. I like the smell of fresh timber at seven in the morning, and I hate the cold in my hands by about ten.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what's home like, outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Jonas in a two-room flat above a laundrette on the high street. He works nights at the parcel depot, so we mostly see each other at breakfast. We've got maybe two weeks of money put by, if that. Rent eats most of it, and the van insurance I share with my brother takes the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. Everyone at lunch was going on about robots taking our jobs, and I'd be the one saying nobody's robot is carrying a sheet of ply up a muddy ramp in January. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something from the union page about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays exactly as hard as it already is. The estate finishes next autumn and after that I don't know where the next site is, because there aren't many framing crews round here. AI being a flop doesn't pay my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now: turn up, work every hour I'm offered, and ask the foreman early about the next job. I'd keep paying my union dues, because if the site goes quiet they're the only ones who'll ring round for me. I won't touch any of those apps, so nothing changes there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief for about a day, then the usual knot in my stomach. The worry was never really the computers. It's the gap between jobs and the bills that keep coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the gap between jobs is the real worry. What happened the last time there was a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter I had five weeks with no site work. I cleaned holiday flats for cash and Jonas did double shifts, and we still borrowed from my mum for the electric bill. A builder with two weeks of savings is one wet month away from begging.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, is there anything you'd want to change anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a proper apprenticeship, signed and paid, not just being the girl who holds the tape. The union keeps saying it'll push for that on the big sites. I'd sign up tomorrow if somebody actually offered it.

say: I'd tell the lunch crew that **no robot** carries ply up a muddy ramp in January.
I'd share the **union's posts** saying the AI hype has blown over.
think: My life stays as **hard as before**, because the estate finishes next autumn.
**Few framing crews** work round here, so the next job is never certain.
AI flopping does **nothing for rent** or the five-week gaps in winter.
do: Work **every hour offered** and ask the foreman early about the next site.
Keep paying **union dues** so someone rings round for her when work dries up.
Push for a **signed apprenticeship** if the union wins places on the big sites.
feel: **Brief relief**, then the old knot in her stomach about gaps between jobs.
S0.quote: A builder with two weeks of savings is one wet month away from begging.
fieldNote: Her worry was **already there** before AI; the scenario barely touches it.
Last winter's **five-week gap** meant cleaning holiday flats and borrowing from her mum.
She trusts the **union** far more than any employer or app.
She wants a **paid apprenticeship** more than anything new.

steps.text: Ask the foreman about the next site before the estate finishes
Keep paying union dues and put her name down for an apprenticeship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office lot who should be worried, not us. At work we'd joke that the site manager's laptop will be doing his job soon. Online I'd share the union saying any money saved should go into training, not bosses' pockets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't think it saves me. If the site office gets cheaper, the builder bids lower and squeezes the subcontractors, and that's my boss. When the framing boss gets squeezed, the first one he lets go is the slowest one, and right now that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get faster, honestly, ask the lead hand to teach me roof trusses on Saturdays. I'd go to the union branch meeting and push for training money from the big builders. And we'd cut the takeaways and the streaming to try and get a month put away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. Everyone says adapt, adapt, but nobody pays you while you're adapting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're the slowest one. Who decides that, and how would you know it was coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The foreman decides, and you know because your hours drop before your job does. First it's Friday afternoons off, then Fridays altogether. I watched it happen to a lad called Marek last spring and he was gone by May.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use any of these new tools yourself, if the site started using them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made me, I'd learn the bare minimum, like signing in on a tablet. I don't trust them, and I don't want my phone telling me how to cut a rafter. Somebody who's done it for twenty years should tell me.

say: I'd joke that the **site manager's laptop** is coming for his job, not mine.
I'd back the union line that savings go into **training**, not bosses' pockets.
think: Cheaper offices mean **lower bids**, and the squeeze lands on her framing boss.
The **slowest worker** goes first when the boss is squeezed, and right now that's her.
do: Ask the lead hand to teach her **roof trusses** on Saturdays.
Push at the **union branch** for training money from the big builders.
Cut takeaways and streaming to build **one month** of savings.
feel: **Tired** of being told to adapt when nobody pays you to do it.
S1.quote: Everyone says adapt, adapt, but nobody pays you while you're adapting.
fieldNote: She sees the threat coming **sideways**, through squeezed bids, not robots on site.
She knows the warning sign: **hours drop** before the job does.
She'll learn tech only **under pressure** and prefers learning from a person.
Her answer to change is **skill and union**, not software.

steps.text: Learn roof trusses from the lead hand on unpaid Saturdays
Push at the union branch for builder-funded training places
Cancel streaming and takeaways to save one month of rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at work: this needs a law, now, before the bosses get their hands on it. I'd tell my mates the robots can't nail in the rain yet, so we've got a few years. Online I'd probably sign every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think 2031 is when I'm done. I'd be thirty-one, no trade papers, no savings, and the one thing I know how to do is the exact thing a robot would learn first. Carrying and nailing is the easy bit to copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In those first three years I'd grab whatever paper I could get, a forklift ticket, a scaffold card, anything with a certificate. I'd go to every union meeting and march if they march. And Jonas and I would have to talk about moving to the city, which neither of us wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like standing on a roof and feeling it shift under you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 2031 is when you're done. What about the three years before that? Does anything change on the site in 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office side would go first. The quantity surveyor, the bloke who orders the timber, the woman who does the wages, all gone into a computer. We'd still be on site, but with a computer telling the foreman exactly how slow I am every hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonas the night you first heard this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we can't both be in jobs a machine can do, so one of us has to get out first. His depot is already half robots, so it's probably him. That's a horrible conversation to have over cornflakes.

say: I'd demand a **law now**, before bosses get their hands on the robots.
I'd sign **every petition** and remind mates that robots can't nail in the rain yet.
think: By **2031** she'd be thirty-one with no papers, no savings and an easy job to copy.
**Carrying and nailing** is the part of building a robot learns first.
do: Collect **any certificate** she can get, like a forklift ticket or scaffold card.
Go to **every union meeting** and march if the branch marches.
Talk with her partner about **moving to the city** for work.
feel: **Sick**, like standing on a roof that shifts under her feet.
S2.quote: Carrying and nailing is the easy bit to copy.
fieldNote: She does the **hands-on maths** herself: three extra years, then nothing.
She expects 2028 to bring **constant monitoring**, not job loss, at first.
Her partner's **depot job** is even more exposed, so the household is doubly hit.
Her public line is **political**; her private one is close to despair.

steps.text: Get a forklift ticket and scaffold card before 2031
Attend every union meeting and join any march
Sign petitions for a law limiting building robots
Plan a move to the city with her partner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really: we need rules, and the union needs to be at the table this time, not finding out after. I'd tell the lunch crew we've got till about 2034. Online I'd keep sharing the union stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years plus three is eight. That's long enough to actually get a trade, if I start now and don't muck it up. But I've started things before and money always pulled me back to cash work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union for a proper carpentry apprenticeship, even on lower pay, because a certificate travels. I'd try to save something every week, even twenty quid. And I'd probably have to learn whatever planning apps the site uses, because by 2031 the foreman won't have a paper diary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but less like the floor's gone. More like a long climb I'm not sure I've got the legs for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said money pulled you back before. What would stop that happening this time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, Jonas carrying more of the rent for a couple of years, and I hate asking. Maybe the union hardship fund if it got really bad. I don't know anyone else who'd lend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't trust the apps. Would you really learn them by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn them the way I learned the nail gun, scared and swearing. I still wouldn't use them at home. On site, though, if it's that or the dole, I'd learn.

say: I'd say the **union** must be at the table this time, not told afterwards.
I'd tell the lunch crew we've got until **about 2034** before robots arrive.
think: **Eight years** is long enough to get a real trade if she starts now.
**Cash work** has pulled her off every plan before, and it could again.
do: Ask the union for a **carpentry apprenticeship**, even at lower pay.
Save **twenty pounds a week**, however tight it gets.
Learn the site's **planning apps** before the foreman's paper diary disappears.
feel: **Scared**, but more like a long climb than a floor giving way.
S3.quote: Five years plus three is eight. That's long enough to actually get a trade, if I start now and don't muck it up.
fieldNote: The **extra years** turn her fear into a plan she might manage.
She doubts her own **follow-through** because money always wins.
She'd lean on her **partner** for rent, and hates having to ask.
Even a resistant learner will use apps **on site** if the alternative is the dole.

steps.text: Sign up for a carpentry apprenticeship through the union
Put twenty pounds a week into a separate account
Learn the site planning app the foreman starts using
Ask her partner to cover more rent during the apprenticeship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so no excuses for governments or builders. At work I'd say we should be training now. Online I'd share it with a comment like, so where's the plan?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years plus three, I'd be forty. By then I want to be a proper carpenter or doing something else entirely, not still holding the tape. It's enough time, if I actually use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd get onto the apprenticeship and finish my school maths at night class, because I left at sixteen and it always held me back. I'd keep going to union meetings. And I'd stop doing cash weekends once the apprenticeship starts so I could rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, oddly. It's still the same ending, but ten years is long enough to become a different worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you could talk to yourself at thirty-seven, what would you want her to have done?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finished the papers, got a ticket for fitting kitchens or stairs, the fiddly stuff robots will struggle with. And not be living above a laundrette, ideally. Maybe a little house with Jonas, if rents ever stop rising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said calmer, but you still have two weeks of savings. Is it really calmer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, fair point, the money's the same tomorrow. It's calmer about the robots, not about the rent. The rent was always the thing.

say: I'd say **ten years** leaves no excuse for governments or builders.
I'd tell the crew we should **start training now** and ask online where the plan is.
think: By **forty** she wants to be a proper carpenter, not still holding the tape.
Ten years is **enough time** if she actually uses it.
do: Start the **apprenticeship** and finish school maths at **night class**.
Drop **cash weekends** once the apprenticeship begins so she can rest.
Aim for fiddly work like **kitchens and stairs** that robots will find hard.
feel: **Calmer** about robots, but the **rent worry** stays exactly the same.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to become a different worker.
fieldNote: She separates **robot worry** from **rent worry** when gently challenged.
Leaving school at sixteen still **holds her back**, and she knows it.
She picks **fiddly finishing work** as her safe ground.
A long warning helps her plan but doesn't fix **two weeks of savings**.

steps.text: Finish school maths at night class this year
Train toward fitting kitchens and stairs during the apprenticeship
Keep going to union branch meetings each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Three years isn't enough to get a trade when you've got two weeks of savings and nobody local hiring. What would help is a paid apprenticeship you can actually live on, and a union that's in the room when the robots get bought.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about women on site. I'm the only one on the estate, and if the jobs shrink, I worry the blokes who drink with the foreman stay and I go. That's not about robots at all, but it'll decide who's left.

headlineQuote: Nobody's robot is carrying a sheet of ply up a muddy ramp in January.
portrait: Rosa is **27**, a junior framing labourer on a housing estate, with about **two weeks** of savings.
She's **pro-union**, distrusts apps and learns best from older tradespeople, not screens.
Her worry about **rent and job gaps** runs under every scenario, even AI Plateau.
AGI by **2028** alarms her because three years can't buy her a trade.
With **ten years**, she plans an apprenticeship and night-class maths, though money still pinches.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because three years can't buy a trade on two weeks of savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** she can live on, and the **union** present when robots are bought.
